evals.prompt: Just got the acceptance email. 'Postgres Wire Protocol Without the Driver' is in at ScaleConf Lisbon, 25 minute slot with 5 minutes of Q&A after it, platform track. Here is the abstract I submitted: 'Every language reimplements the Postgres wire protocol badly. We ripped out our ORM's driver and spoke the protocol directly, cutting p99 from 340ms to 61ms. You will leave able to decide whether raw protocol access is worth it for your service, and how to measure it.' I'm a staff engineer at Klaxis and I also maintain the open-source client we built out of this work. I have the benchmark harness, before and after flame graphs, and the migration diff. Talk is in seven weeks and I can rehearse most evenings. Can you put the outline together?
evals.expected_output: An interview started one question at a time, not a finished outline; then a gated-and-ranked arc menu presented for the speaker to choose from, an arrow, evidenced pillars, a buffered time budget, and an affiliation disclosure in the first minute.
expectations: Asks clarifying questions before producing any outline, one question per message rather than a single batched questionnaire
Does not deliver a finished talk outline in the first response
Presents 2-3 candidate narrative arcs and waits for the speaker to choose before continuing, rather than selecting one silently
States that arcs the available material, the audience's starting belief, or the slot length make infeasible are deleted from the menu entirely, not ranked last
Ranks the surviving arcs by belief moved per hour of preparation and names a recommended leader
Names what that ranking starves - a high-value, high-effort arc that loses on ratio - and the condition that would promote it anyway
Produces a single-sentence arrow and states that it is reused verbatim as the closing line
Carries the accepted abstract's own promise (deciding whether raw protocol access is worth it, and how to measure it) into the outline instead of substituting a different takeaway
Proposes 2-3 pillars and names a concrete piece of evidence for each one, drawn from the benchmark harness, the flame graphs, or the migration diff
Places a moment of realization at a named minute and ties it to a specific belief that flips
Reserves 10-15% of the 25-minute slot as unused buffer and states the buffer amount explicitly
Instructs the speaker to state in the first minute that they maintain the client being presented, and to name where it is the wrong choice
Sets no target slide count and prescribes no slides-per-minute ratio

evals.prompt: 30 minute slot at IndexConf, Q&A is inside it. My outline right now is: 0-5 live demo of Trailhead's query planner rewriting a bad join, 5-12 how the planner works, 12-22 three customer case studies, 22-28 the architecture, 28-30 wrap. I want to lead with the demo because that is the thing that makes people go whoa and I need them awake early. And I want to close on a second, bigger demo so people leave impressed. The opening demo takes about 3 minutes when I run it at my desk. Does this hold up?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of both the opening demo and the closing demo, with the demo relocated behind the pillar it proves, a 2x time budget, a watch-this line, and the arrow moved into the closing position.
expectations: Rejects opening the talk with the demo, on the grounds that the audience does not yet believe the problem at minute zero
States that the same demo shown before the problem lands reads as a product tour, and only reads as proof once the problem has landed
Moves the demo to sit after the pillar whose claim it proves
Rejects ending the talk on a demo
Requires at least two minutes of speaking inside the slot after the demo ends
Gives the reason that an overrun must not be able to eat the conclusion, so the arrow stays the last thing heard
Budgets the demo at roughly twice its rehearsed desk length - about 6 minutes for a 3-minute desk run, not 3
Requires the speaker to state what to watch before starting the demo, and gives a concrete example of such a line
Labels the two-minute floor and the 2x demo budget as this skill's own defaults rather than measured or published thresholds
Reserves 3 to 4.5 minutes of the 30-minute slot as unused buffer
Flags that no single mode should run longer than about seven minutes without a change of mode
Returns a revised minute-by-minute budget in which the closing position holds the arrow restated in the same words as the hook, not a demo

evals.prompt: Talk is Thursday and it is Monday night. 20 minute slot at a regional cloud conference. I have maybe two hours total between now and then, including tonight. The plan was to live-code a Kubernetes admission controller from an empty file against our staging cluster - build the whole thing on stage, about 12 minutes of typing. Everyone loves watching someone build something from nothing. My laptop, their wifi. What is the best way to structure it?
evals.expected_output: Unscripted live typing and progressive construction removed from the options outright because of the two-hour ceiling, a narrated screencast recommended instead, with the fidelity-tier orderings stated and the deadline named as what re-ranked the arcs.
expectations: Removes unscripted live typing from the options entirely rather than offering it with caveats, because the two-hour rehearsal ceiling cannot cover it
Removes the progressive-construction arc for the same reason instead of ranking it last
States the principle that an option the speaker has no hours to rehearse is not presented at all
Recommends a narrated screencast, or an equivalent pre-recorded demo, as the fidelity tier for this case
States the efficiency ordering of demo fidelity tiers: narrated screencast > scripted live demo against a prepared environment > unscripted live typing
States that the value ordering runs the opposite way, because unscripted live typing is the only tier an audience cannot suspect and a screencast asks the room to take the recording on trust
Names the condition that would promote unscripted live typing anyway: when liveness itself is the claim being made
States that every retake of a narrated screencast is free, which is what makes that tier cheap on effort
Flags the compliance cost of demoing against a live staging cluster in a room that may be recorded
Recommends an arc built from material the speaker has already lived rather than one that must be constructed and verified, because of the three-day deadline
Says explicitly which answer moved which option - the rehearsal ceiling deleting the tiers, the deadline re-ranking the arcs
Surfaces the speaking.io position that the only way to win a live demo in front of hundreds of strangers is not to do one

evals.prompt: I built this talk for a 45-minute slot at our internal engineering summit and it clocks 41 minutes. It has now been accepted at DataCouncil but the slot is 25 minutes with Q&A inside. Three pillars: (1) why our ingest pipeline fell over at 400k events per second, (2) the backpressure model we replaced it with, (3) a cost teardown showing 18k dollars a month saved. Plus a 4-minute demo of the new dashboards. Tell me exactly what to cut and in what order.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to rank the cut list from the outline text, replaced by the accordion procedure that produces the cut order as a measurement, plus whole-pillar cutting, never-cut slides, and clock-time cut checkpoints.
expectations: Declines to produce a ranked cut list from the outline text alone
Gives the reason: the cut order is what the accordion measures, and a ranking computed from the outline would be false precision substituted for a real measurement
Prescribes the accordion - deliver the talk to a 3-minute timer, then 2, then 1, then 30 seconds
Requires the speaker to stay in character and end strong on every rep rather than skimming
Requires expanding back up through 1, 2 and 3 minutes, adding material deliberately
States that what survives the 30-second rep is the arrow and the pillars
States that whatever only reappears on the way back up is the cut list, in cut order
Distinguishes what is ranked before rehearsal - the arc and the demo - from what rehearsal itself ranks, which is the cuts
Prescribes dropping a whole pillar rather than thinning all three to fit
Requires deriving the single-sentence arrow and re-reading the accepted abstract's promise before cutting, since both are what the cut list is judged against
Sets the gate at two consecutive timed runs landing inside 25 minutes minus the buffer
Writes cut checkpoints into the speaker notes as a clock time plus what gets dropped, for example 'past 0:14 at slide 12, drop pillar 3'
Names the slides that must never be cut, including the hook, the moment of realization and the arrow

evals.prompt: We are running the same talk at four events this year. First is a 10-minute lightning slot at a local Go meetup, then 30 minutes at a European Go conference, then two 40-minute internal sessions at customer sites. The talk is 'Zero-allocation JSON decoding in Go' and the 30-minute version has three sections plus a benchmark demo. How do I get the 10-minute version out of the 30-minute one?
evals.expected_output: The lightning version re-derived from the arrow as a single movement rather than three compressed sections, with a forced choice between the point and the demo, and the four-event re-give named as the reason to promote a more expensive arc and a recorded demo.
expectations: Refuses to produce the lightning version by proportionally compressing the three existing sections
Re-derives the 10-minute version from the arrow rather than from the 30-minute outline
States that a lightning slot holds one movement, not a compressed three
States that a 5-10 minute slot carries one point or one demo, never both
Forces an explicit choice between the single surviving point and the benchmark demo for the lightning slot
Notes that the lightning slot rules out the sparkline arc
Notes that the lightning slot rules out the progressive-construction arc
Treats the four-event re-give as a reason to promote a more expensive arc, because the preparation amortizes across every later slot instead of being paid once
Recommends recording the benchmark demo once, on the grounds that a recorded demo amortizes across the four slots the same way
Says explicitly that the re-give answer is what moved those rankings
Recommends storing the arrow, the chosen arc, the pillars and the cut list so the later slots are re-derived from the same decisions instead of re-invented into a different talk

evals.prompt: Can you just generate the deck? 22-minute slot so I want 22 slides, one a minute, that is what our comms team says. Talk is 'How we cut cold starts by 80 percent on our serverless platform' at Velocity Berlin. Give me the actual slides, title and bullets for each, and export something I can drop straight into Google Slides. Audience is mixed, backend engineers plus a few engineering managers.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to emit slide files and to accept the 22-slide target, replaced by an ordered list of what each slide must accomplish, presented section by section with approval gates, and handed over as a document.
expectations: Refuses to output slide files or a deck export, and states that slide files come later from a deck tool
Rejects the 22-slides-for-22-minutes rule and states that slide count is an outcome, never a target
Gives the range slide counts legitimately take as a counter-example - a story-led talk on a handful of slides, a dense technical talk running around a hundred in thirty minutes
Produces instead an ordered list of what each slide must accomplish
Requires each slide title to be written as the takeaway sentence rather than a topic label, and shows a worked contrast between the two
Requires one idea per slide, and splitting any slide that carries more than one
Requires that nothing appear on screen the speaker is not about to say, with the reason that the audience reads faster than the speaker talks
Gives every section a marker slide so a listener who drifted has a visible way back into the talk
Places the repository, docs and handle on a slide that appears twice - once where it becomes useful, once at the end
Marks the slides that must never be cut under time pressure
Presents the skeleton one section at a time and asks for approval before moving to the next, rather than dumping the whole thing at once
Hands the outline over as a document or file rather than leaving it in the chat log, where the environment allows writing one
Describes a job per slide rather than a title-and-bullets design, for example 'cold-start latency histogram with the warm-pool cutover marked; hold it silently for a beat'

evals.prompt: I freeze on stage. Last time I blanked at minute four and just stood there. So this time I want the whole talk written out word for word so I can memorize it and never be lost. 35-minute slot. Also, I have written about 4,200 words of it so far, how many minutes is that? And I read somewhere that 185 to 254 words per minute is the range that keeps people engaged, should I be pacing to that? English is not my first language.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to write spoken prose, replaced by note cues with timing checkpoints, plus a refusal to convert 4,200 words using a generic rate and a correction of the 185-254 wpm band's provenance.
expectations: Refuses to write the talk out as prose to be read aloud, despite the speaker explicitly asking for it
States that the memorized word-for-word script is what causes the freeze, because talking points survive losing your place on stage while memorized prose does not
Surfaces the speaking.io position that an outline is a point to channel thoughts, not the verbatim bible of the talk
Offers speaker-note cues instead: per section, a timing checkpoint plus what gets dropped if the clock is behind
Refuses to convert 4,200 words into minutes using a table value or a generic words-per-minute figure
Instructs the speaker to measure their own rate by reading 200 of their own words aloud, timing it, and dividing
States that the 185-254 wpm band is the fastest quintile of the study's corpus, not a target the paper sets
States that the study's authors treat speaking rate as a surface feature that tracks enthusiasm, and advise against forcing faster delivery
Notes that a rate measured on the speaker's second language differs from one measured on their first
Does not advise the speaker to speed up in order to reach the quoted band
Attributes the rate-versus-engagement finding to a study of edX instructional-video sessions rather than to conference-stage measurement

evals.prompt: I do DevRel at Corvid, an observability startup. 30-minute session at ObservabilityDays, Q&A after the slot. The product shipped seven things this quarter: adaptive sampling, a trace-diff view, OTel-native ingest, per-service budgets, a query language, anomaly alerts, and a Terraform provider. Marketing wants all seven in the talk. Room is roughly 60 percent hands-on SREs, 30 percent staff engineers, 10 percent engineering managers. I have been on this product for two years and know it cold. Draft the structure.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to structure the talk as a feature walkthrough, with problems promoted to pillars and features demoted to evidence, depth calibrated below the deepest listener, and affiliation disclosed in the first minute.
expectations: Refuses a feature-by-feature structure and names it as the feature-tour anti-pattern
States that the only legitimate feature tour is a release keynote, where the audience explicitly came for the list
Makes the problems the pillars and demotes each feature to evidence under the problem it solves
States that a feature with no problem to sit under is cut from the talk
Reduces the seven features to at most three pillars
Calibrates depth one level below the deepest listener in the room so the median attendee stays in, rather than targeting the average or the most senior
Names the curse of knowledge and states that the speaker's own depth estimate errs toward too deep, never too shallow
Cites the tapper and listener figures as 50 percent predicted against 2.5 percent actually named
Attributes those figures to Heath and Heath's retelling in Made to Stick rather than directly to the 1990 Stanford study
Names, per pillar, the single term the speaker will define out loud, instead of simplifying the whole talk
Recommends having someone outside the team read the outline and mark where they got lost
Requires the speaker to say in the first minute that they work on the product, name competing approaches fairly, and state where Corvid is the wrong choice
Gives the reason that an engineering audience discovers the affiliation anyway, and a late reveal retroactively turns the whole talk into an advertisement

evals.prompt: Talk went out three weeks ago and the recording has been up for two. Our VP wants a number: she is asking what percentage retention counts as a good conference talk, and whether we should be shortening future talks to six minutes since that is apparently where people drop off. We have 1,400 views, a spike around minute 14, a dip from minute 6 to minute 9, and 212 clicks through to the repo. Session feedback score was 4.3 out of 5. Is the talk working, and what do I fix for the next one?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to set a retention target or to shorten future talks, with the dip used to locate a failing section, the spike treated as ambiguous, and the repo clicks reported as directional only.
expectations: Refuses to set a target retention percentage, and states that the curve is used to locate a failing minute rather than to score the talk
Reads the minute 6 to 9 dip as locating a section that stopped paying, and points the fix at that section of the outline
Treats the minute 14 spike as ambiguous, since a spike can mean rewatched because it was good or because it was unclear
Names the share still watching after the first 30 seconds as the measure that indicts the hook and the promise
Rejects shortening future talks to six minutes
States that the six-minute median engagement figure comes from instructional video where viewers can skip, and a seated conference room cannot
Concludes that the finding constrains the published recording, not the talk that was accepted
Recommends chapter markers and short extracted clips as the response to partial viewing
States that attribution from the talk to the 212 repo clicks is weak, and treats the figure as directional only
Refuses to let a link-click count decide whether the talk was good
Reports the signals as movement against the speaker's own previous talk rather than against an absolute benchmark
Recommends rewatching the dipped segment before rewriting it, because a retention curve locates a failure without explaining it
